extracted.intended_audience: IB Language and Literature HL students (First Assessment 2026) and their teachers at West Sound Academy
extracted.subtask_short: IB Language A HL assessment prep
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for the four HL assessment components (Paper 1, Paper 2, HL Essay, Individual Oral) plus supporting materials (Learner Portfolio, text classification, and choosing global issues) for the IB Language and Literature course (First Assessment 2026).

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper 1: Guided Textual Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Time: 2 hours 15 minutes. Weight: 35% of your final grade. Type: External assessment. Texts: Two previously unseen non-literary texts of different types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You will be given two non-literary passages (for example, ads, speeches, articles, etc.), each with a guiding question. Your task is to write a detailed analysis of both texts, showing how they communicate meaning through language, structure, and style. (Advice implied: close reading of language, structure and stylistic devices; address both texts; manage time for two responses.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper 2: Comparative Essay
rubrics_metrics.description: Time: 1 hour 45 minutes. Weight: 25% of your final grade. Type: External assessment. Texts: Two literary works you’ve studied (not used in your individual oral or HL essay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You’ll choose one of four general questions and write a comparative essay using two literary works from your course. Show how themes, techniques, and ideas connect across texts (comparative focus, textual evidence, synthesis of similarities/differences).

rubrics_metrics.name: HL Essay (Higher Level Essay)
rubrics_metrics.description: Length: 1,200–1,500 words. Weight: 20% of your final grade. Type: External assessment. Texts: One literary or non-literary work you’ve studied (not used in your individual oral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You’ll write a formal essay exploring a deeper idea or concept in one of your studied works. This is a chance to dive into a topic that really interests you and show off your analytical skills (sustained argument, focused research/interpretation, appropriate length constraint).

rubrics_metrics.name: Individual Oral (IO)
rubrics_metrics.description: Time: 15 minutes total (10-minute presentation + 5-minute Q&A). Weight: 20% of your final grade. Type: Internal assessment. Texts: One literary work and one non-literary body of work (not used in your HL essay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You’ll prepare a spoken response to a global issue of your choice, using one literary and one non-literary work to explore how that issue is presented through content and form. After your presentation, your teacher will ask a few follow-up questions. Practical requirements implied: choose relevant extracts, prepare timing for a 10-minute presentation, anticipate teacher questions in Q&A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global issue: qualification criteria for the Individual Oral
rubrics_metrics.description: To qualify as a global issue your chosen issue must: (1) Have significance on a wide scale — it affects many people or societies, not just a small group; (2) Be transnational — it crosses borders and is relevant in multiple countries or regions; (3) Impact everyday life — even though it’s global, it should also be felt in local, personal contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guide provides five broad fields of inquiry to help brainstorm (Culture, Identity and Community; Beliefs, Values and Education; Politics, Power and Justice; Art, Creativity and Imagination; Science, Technology and Environment) with example focus areas (e.g., race, gender, human rights, censorship, climate change). Advice: don’t pick an overly broad category (e.g., 'gender'); instead define a specific issue (example: 'the impact of gender norms on professional identity across cultures'). Suggested sources: Gale in Context: Global Issues, UN Sustainable Development Goals, and accompanying school guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Making the Individual Oral work: selection and analytical preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical steps to prepare the IO: Select two texts (one literary and one non-literary) that clearly show the chosen global issue; choose extracts from each text that provide strong evidence; be ready to analyse how the authors use language, structure, and style to explore the issue; show how the issue is presented in both texts and how it connects to the real world (locally and globally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on selecting clear, well-evidenced extracts and focusing analysis on content and form. (Implied assessment criteria: clarity of issue, textual evidence, formal analysis, linkage between texts and to real-world implications.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Learner Portfolio: purpose, contents, format and final requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The Learner Portfolio is an evolving, personal record of ideas and responses built over two years; it is not directly graded by the IB but is essential for preparing assessments and showing development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose: track learning journey, reflect on texts, make connections between texts/concepts/real-world issues, prepare for assessments, develop critical thinking/research/self-management skills. Contents: mix of formal and informal responses (reflections and analysis, connections and exploration, creative/experimental work, preparation for assessments such as annotated extracts and practice Paper 1 responses, self-assessment and feedback). Format: digital or paper-based, traditional or multimedia, structured or freeform — teacher will provide templates and feedback. Final requirement: portfolio must include a Works Studied Form listing all texts engaged and how they connect to assessments. Tips: start early, update regularly, be honest and reflective, use it to experiment and grow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary vs Non-literary texts: classification rules and examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Lists of text types considered literary (graphic novel, poem, novel, short story, novella, song lyrics, play) and non-literary (advertisement, infographic, appeal, interview, blog, music video, brochure/leaflet, photograph, cartoon, radio broadcast, diagram, report, electronic text, screenplay for TV/film, encyclopedia entry, set of instructions, film/television, textbook, guide book, work of art). There is also a list of text types that could be either (autobiography/biography, memoir, diary entry content, opinion column, essay, parody, letter, pastiche, magazine article, speech, manifesto, travelogue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: How to decide if a text is literary: If the text is written by an author on the IB Prescribed Reading List or someone known for their literary work, it is literary. If the text has a clear artistic or aesthetic purpose (using creative language, structure, or style to express ideas), it is literary. If it doesn’t meet either of those criteria, it is non-literary. (Use these rules when selecting texts for assessments and the Works Studied Form.)

rubrics_metrics.name: General assessment skills and study advice
rubrics_metrics.description: Each component is designed to test different skills—from close reading and analysis to comparison, argumentation, and oral communication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final tips provided: stay organized, plan ahead, choose works and topics that genuinely interest you, and use your teacher as your best resource. Suggested tools/links for preparation and academic integrity: school database access, Grammarly, NoodleTools, PlagiarismCheck.org.
